# Abstract

This paper reconstructs the demographic trajectory of Mongolia from the terminal Pleistocene to the imperial unification under Genghis Khan in 1206AD under JADE-I. Across six primary hydrographic and ecological basins covering 1.562.476 km² (26.461 five-arcminute grid cells), aggregate human numbers expanded from an Epipalaeolithic baseline of 15k (15.000) in 10000BC to 28k in 6000BC, accelerated across the Bronze Age pastoral transition to 85k in 2000BC and 165k in 1000BC, reached 420k during the Xiongnu imperial floruit in 0AD, and attained 700k at the 1206AD Kurultai [@Jeong2020Dynamic; @dicosmo2002ancient; @honeychurch2014inner].

Growth across the eastern Eurasian steppe followed structural transformations in mobile livestock husbandry, monument construction and supratribal political organisation rather than urban demographic accumulation [@Taylor2020Early; @rogers2012inner]. The Bronze Age adoption of ruminant and horse dairying sustained dense valley occupations without permanent towns [@Jeong2018Bronze; @J2025Slab], while imperial statecraft under the Xiongnu, Turks, Uyghurs and Khitan Liao introduced fortified nodal citadels, agricultural garrisons and craft centres such as Khar Balgas (peaking at 48k), Chin Tolgoi (14k) and Kherlen Bars (11k) [@bemmann2011complex; @barfield1989perilous]. Sub-regional spatial densities are modelled using Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging calibrated across 87.810 East Asian domestic site counts and 1.074 catchments (regularised $\tau_1 = 1,50$, $\tau_2 = 2,775$, nugget-to-sill 0,04, residual $R^2 = 0,9994$) combined with 437 catalogued settlements and monument complexes (2.795 settlement-year observations, mean 6,40 per centre) integrating archaeological excavation registers, OSM/Wikidata Mongolian archaeological sites, river-valley pastoral encampment loci and Zenodo Early China and Steppe radiocarbon records [@paciorek2006spatial; @Taylor2019Radiocarbon; @EarlyChinaC14_2025].

# Background

## Steppe Ecology and Pastoral Carrying Capacity

The Mongolian Plateau occupies an extreme continental semi-arid environment bounded by the Siberian boreal taiga to the north, the Altai ranges to the west, and the hyper-arid Gobi depression to the south [@Lerch2022Holocene]. Mean annual precipitation grades steeply from more than 350 mm in the northern forest-steppe corridors of the Selenge, Orkhon and Tuul rivers down to less than 100 mm in the Southern Gobi, creating sharply contrasting baseline carrying capacities across the six primary hydro-basins [@M2025Bioavailable]. In hyper-arid desert-steppe and dry gravel plains, nomadic pastoralism requires expansive grazing circuits, seasonal herd dispersal and reliance on camels and caprines, keeping regional human densities below 0,16 persons per km² throughout prehistory [@Almathen2016Ancient; @Bennett2017Taming].

By contrast, the alluvial corridors of the Orkhon-Selenge basin and the intermontane valleys of the Khangai highlands provide well-watered river terraces, productive meadow grasses and sheltered mountain winter pastures that insulate livestock herds against catastrophic winter blizzards (*dzud*) [@Lerch2022Holocene; @houle2010emergent]. These central and northern basins functioned as the persistent ecological epicentre of pastoral demography and political centralization [@honeychurch2014inner; @dicosmo2002ancient]. Human densities in the Orkhon-Selenge basin grew from 0,02 persons per km² in 10000BC to 0,50 in 200BC and reached 1,24 persons per km² by 1206AD, absorbing more than 40% of the entire plateau population.

Pastoral survival in this volatile environment depended upon maintaining a balanced multispecies herd, traditionally conceptualised as the five snouts (*tavan khoshuu mal*): horses, cattle and yaks, sheep, goats and Bactrian camels [@A2025Patterns; @AR2022Spread]. Each species fulfilled distinct ecological and economic functions. Sheep provided the primary caloric foundation of mutton, tallow, milk and felt insulation for yurts; goats contributed cashmere, milk and drought resilience; cattle and yaks furnished high-volume dairy yields and heavy draught power for moving four-wheeled ox-carts; horses supplied cavalry mobility, status displays and fermented mare's milk (*airag*); and two-humped Bactrian camels provided indispensable transport across dry gravel terrain [@Almathen2016Ancient; @Bennett2017Taming; @S2024Cauldrons].

Seasonal mobility cycles dictated the spatial distribution of pastoral households across the annual round [@A2025Patterns; @houle2010emergent]. Pastoralists dispersed across open upland summer pastures to exploit flush vegetative growth, congregated along riparian meadows in autumn, and withdrew into protected mountain valleys during harsh winter months [@A2025Patterns]. This rhythmic oscillation (*otor*) prevented pasture degradation while placing strict ceilings on local population density [@sneath2007headless]. Dendroclimatic reconstructions from Khangai Siberian larch series demonstrate that multi-year droughts and extreme frost events caused severe livestock die-offs, triggering acute inter-tribal competition over sheltered winter camps and hay meadows [@Schulte2022Larix; @Lerch2022Holocene].

## The Neolithic Horizon and the Bronze Age Dairy Revolution

During the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene (10000BC to 6000BC), small populations of microblade hunter-gatherers occupied river margins and lake shores, subsisting on wild ungulates, fish and riparian plant resources [@Zhang2025Genomic; @Schulte2022Larix]. Aggregate numbers grew slowly from 15k to 28k over four millennia. Between 6000BC and 3000BC, mid-Holocene climatic warming supported broad-spectrum foraging adaptations and localized pottery manufacture along the eastern steppe margins without generating sedentary agricultural villages [@Chen2026Broad; @Sun2025Multi].

The crucial demographic rupture occurred around 3000BC with the introduction of western Eurasian livestock pastoralism [@Jeong2018Bronze; @Haak2015Massive]. Genomic and dental calculus palaeoproteomic investigations demonstrate that Afanasievo-related pastoralists introduced domesticated sheep, goats and cattle into western and central Mongolia between 3000BC and 2500BC [@Jeong2018Bronze; @K2026Ancient; @AR2022Spread]. The consumption of ruminant dairy products expanded the caloric carrying capacity of open steppe grasslands, decoupling human subsistence from wild game densities and initiating sustained demographic growth [@Taylor2020Early; @Wilkin2020Dairy]. Total population advanced from 50k in 3000BC to 85k in 2000BC and reached 165k by 1000BC.

From 1400BC onward, the Deer Stone-Khirigsuur Complex (DSKC) across northern and central Mongolia and the contemporary Slab Grave culture across the eastern steppe constructed monumental stone mortuary landscapes that required coordinated communal labour [@Taylor2019Radiocarbon; @J2025Slab; @houle2010emergent]. Thousands of ritual stone mounds (*khirigsuurs*) with peripheral horse sacrifice rings demonstrate the full integration of mounted horsemanship, equine milking and specialized seasonal transhumance [@D2026Horse; @S2024Cauldrons; @A2025Patterns]. Isotopic analyses of horse remains from ritual contexts confirm seasonal herd management and long-distance mobility across the Altai and Khangai mountains [@A2025Patterns; @AR2022Spread]. This Bronze Age pastoral regime supported robust natural increase, raising plateau population to 260k by 500BC.

The transition from the Bronze Age to the early Iron Age witnessed increasing ideological and economic differentiation between eastern and western pastoralists [@J2025Slab]. While central and western communities maintained the monumental khirigsuur tradition, eastern groups developed the Slab Grave mortuary tradition, characterized by rectangular stone slabs oriented east-west [@J2025Slab]. Ancient genomic data demonstrate that around 800BC, Slab Grave populations expanded westward into the Khangai highlands, assimilating earlier pastoral lineages and establishing the genetic baseline for later nomadic confederations [@J2025Slab; @Jeong2020Dynamic].

## Deer Stone Megaliths and Mortuary Coordination

The physical expression of Bronze Age social coordination appears most dramatically in carved deer stones (*maral chuluu*), standing granite stelae measuring up to four metres in height [@Taylor2019Radiocarbon; @houle2010emergent]. More than 1.200 deer stones are documented across Mongolia, concentrated heavily in the Khangai and Khövsgöl valleys [@Taylor2019Radiocarbon]. The stelae are carved with flying deer featuring elongated, bird-like beaks and sweeping curvilinear antlers, accompanied by stylized representations of weapons, daggers, bows, quivers, shields and solar discs [@houle2010emergent].

These megaliths were not isolated grave markers; rather, they formed focal nodes in complex ceremonial landscapes [@Taylor2019Radiocarbon]. Khirigsuurs frequently comprise a central stone cairn surrounded by a circular or rectangular boulder fence, outside of which lie dozens or hundreds of small stone cists containing sacrificed horse crania and cervical vertebrae oriented toward the rising sun [@Taylor2019Radiocarbon; @A2025Patterns]. Spatial analyses in the Khanuy Valley indicate that such monument complexes functioned as territorial aggregation points where dispersed pastoral lineages gathered seasonally to reaffirm political alliances, negotiate pasture rights and conduct elite funerary rituals [@houle2010emergent].

## Skeletal Frailty and Pastoral Demography

Bioarchaeological investigations of Bronze Age and Iron Age skeletal series provide vital constraints on demographic models of fertility, mortality and health on the steppe [@Jeong2018Bronze; @J2025Slab]. Skeletal remains from Khangai khirigsuurs and Slab Grave cemeteries reveal low frequencies of dental caries, consistent with high-protein, low-carbohydrate pastoral diets dominated by milk and meat rather than refined cereal flours [@Wilkin2020Dairy; @Zhang2021Pastoralism].

However, high rates of dental wear, periodontal disease and calculus accumulation attest to coarse food textures and dust contamination common in dry steppe camps [@Wilkin2020Dairy]. Skeletal stress markers, notably *cribra orbitalia* and linear enamel hypoplasias, occur in 20% to 35% of analysed individuals, reflecting seasonal nutritional shortages and episodic parasitic infections [@Jeong2018Bronze]. Trauma patterns reveal frequent healed fractures of the clavicle, ribs and lower limbs, characteristic of falls from horses, alongside cranial injuries consistent with hand-to-hand combat in inter-lineage raids [@D2026Horse; @houle2010emergent]. Life expectancy at birth is estimated at 26 to 30 years, with adult life expectancy clustering in the fourth and fifth decades [@Jeong2020Dynamic].

## Imperial Consolidation and Nomadic Statehood

The rise of the Xiongnu Empire under Modun Chanyu around 209BC transformed the political geography of Inner Asia [@dicosmo2002ancient; @brosseder2011xiongnu]. In response to the unified Qin and Han empires in China, the Xiongnu organised a centralized hierarchical state divided into Left, Central and Right administrative wings, exercising authority over nomadic pastoralists and sedentary enclaves [@barfield1989perilous; @sneath2007headless]. Archaeological excavations at Noyon Uul, Gol Mod 1, Gol Mod 2 and Burkhan Tolgoi reveal unprecedented social differentiation, monumental wooden terrace tombs, imported Chinese silks, bronze mirrors and lacquer vessels alongside local craft production [@brosseder2011xiongnu; @A2026Ancient].

To provision court elites and cavalry retinues, the Xiongnu established fortified valley settlements and agricultural colonies at Boroo Gol, Gua Dov and Tereljiin Dorvoljin, where captive Han artisans and farmers grew proso and foxtail millet [@Zhang2021Pastoralism; @honeychurch2014inner]. These enclaves diversified the steppe caloric base, lifting aggregate numbers to 380k in 200BC and an imperial peak of 420k in 0AD. Economic stability was heavily reinforced through negotiated peace treaties (*heqin*) with the Han court, which transferred tens of thousands of bolts of silk, thousand bushels of grain and gold coinage directly into the Chanyu's treasury [@dicosmo2002ancient; @barfield1989perilous]. These external subsidies allowed Xiongnu rulers to redistribute prestige goods to subordinate clan leaders without levying crippling internal taxes on pastoral herds [@barfield1989perilous].

Han military expeditions, internal succession schisms and devastating droughts triggered the fragmentation of the Xiongnu into northern and southern branches in the first century AD, producing demographic contraction to 360k by 200AD [@dicosmo2002ancient; @barfield1989perilous]. Succeeding confederations—the Xianbei under Tanshihuai (ca. 156-181AD) and the Rouran Khaganate (ca. 330-552AD)—maintained mobile imperial structures but faced chronic internal instability, holding total population between 360k and 390k [@barfield1989perilous; @golden1992introduction]. Tanshihuai organized the Xianbei into tripartite divisions modeled on the Xiongnu, but his realm disintegrated rapidly upon his death, demonstrating the frailty of imperial structures without permanent administrative nodes [@barfield1989perilous]. The Rouran dominated the steppe for two centuries through tributary extractions from the Northern Wei and control over Oasis city-states in the Tarim Basin [@golden1992introduction].

In 552AD, the Göktürks overthrew the Rouran, establishing the First and Second Turkic Khaganates from their sacred headquarters in the Ötüken mountain forest-steppe of the Khangai highlands [@golden1992introduction]. Turkic funerary complexes with anthropomorphic stelae and Orkhon runic inscriptions at Khoshoo Tsaidam (Bilge Khagan and Kül Tegin) reflected an imperial ideology that balanced nomadic military discipline with extensive tribute extraction across Eurasian trade arteries [@golden1992introduction]. Ashina rulers mobilized vast cavalry divisions, regularised pastoral territorial boundaries, and fostered trade along the northern branches of the Silk Road, elevating plateau numbers to 470k.

The Uyghur Khaganate (744AD to 840AD) expanded urbanisation on the steppe to unprecedented scale [@bemmann2011complex; @rogers2012inner]. Abandoning pure nomadism at the elite level, the Uyghur court embraced Sogdian Manichaeism and constructed the colossal walled capital of Khar Balgas (Ordu-Baliq) on the Orkhon River, enclosing palaces, temples, craft workshops and residential districts over 25 km² [@bemmann2011complex]. Together with regional garrison towns like Baibalyk on the Selenge, Khar Balgas sustained an urban agglomeration of 48k residents, lifting plateau population to 490k in 750AD.

Following the violent sack of Khar Balgas by the Yenisei Kyrgyz in 840AD, the Khitan Liao Dynasty (907-1125AD) annexed central and eastern Mongolia, establishing a fortified frontier administration [@barfield1989perilous; @sneath2007headless]. The Liao constructed large earthen walled fortresses and garrison towns—most notably Chin Tolgoi (14k peak), Kherlen Bars (11k peak), Khar Bukh Balgas (7,5k) and Khermen Denzh (5,5k)—manned by Khitan garrisons, Bohai and Han agricultural settlers, and Buddhist monastic institutions [@bemmann2011complex]. When the Liao collapsed before the Jurchen Jin dynasty around 1125AD, these garrisons reverted to local pastoral polities. Decades of competitive militarisation among the Khamag Mongol, Kereit, Naiman, Merkit and Tatar confederations culminated in the elevation of Temüjin as Genghis Khan at the 1206AD Kurultai on the Onon River, uniting a population of 700k mobile pastoralists and warrior retinues [@barfield1989perilous; @honeychurch2014inner].

## Frontier Fortifications and Caravan Networks

Steppe empires maintained complex territorial defense networks designed to monitor pastoral movements and secure trans-Eurasian trade routes [@honeychurch2014inner; @barfield1989perilous]. During the Xiongnu and Han confrontations, border wall systems, earthen ramparts and beacon towers extended along the northern edges of the Gobi desert, functioning as early warning infrastructure against surprise cavalry raids [@dicosmo2002ancient].

These defensive corridors also facilitated the movement of commercial caravans [@golden1992introduction]. Sogdian merchants, establishing trading colonies across the Orkhon and Tuul valleys, served as diplomatic emissaries, financial managers and scribes for Turkic and Uyghur khagans [@golden1992introduction; @bemmann2011complex]. The integration of caravan waystations, garrison fortresses and pastoral winter camps formed an administrative network that linked the Mongolian Plateau directly to the oasis city-states of the Silk Road and the imperial capitals of northern China [@honeychurch2014inner].

# Methodology

## Hydrographic Partition and Spatial Scope

The JADE-I module partitions Mongolia (1.562.476 km² across 26.461 five-arcminute grid cells) into six primary hydrographic and ecological basins:
1. Orkhon-Selenge Forest-Steppe Basin (168.883 km²): northern alluvial drainage of the Selenge, lower Orkhon and Tuul rivers.
2. Khangai Central Highlands and Tamir-Khanuy (210.992 km²): central mountain forest-steppe, upper Orkhon, Tamir and Khanuy valleys.
3. Kherlen-Onon Eastern Steppe Basin (299.514 km²): eastern rolling plains draining toward the Amur-Pacific basin.
4. Altai Mountains and Great Lakes Depression (297.051 km²): western mountain chains and endorheic lake basins.
5. Southern Gobi Desert-Steppe and Oases (496.815 km²): arid southern plains and intermittent oasis corridors.
6. Lake Khövsgöl and Darkhad Boreal Taiga (89.221 km²): northern sub-arctic taiga, alpine valleys and mountain rift lakes.

At each benchmark year $t \in [-10000, 1206]$, total population $P(t)$ represents the sum of regional population estimates $P_r(t)$ across all six basins:

$$P(t) = \sum_{r=1}^{6} P_r(t)$$

Each regional baseline $P_r(t)$ integrates archaeological radiocarbon sample densities, zooarchaeological livestock counts, settlement spatial extents and historical tributary records compiled from epigraphic and dynastic sources [@Jeong2020Dynamic; @Taylor2019Radiocarbon; @dicosmo2002ancient]. Across Mongolia, the spatial gazetteer incorporates 437 validated centres (2.795 settlement-year observations, mean 6,40 per centre), reconciled from 645 evaluated ledger candidates (208 excluded duplicates or unconfirmed scatters, 0 unaccounted) after integrating OSM/Wikidata Mongolian archaeological sites, river-valley pastoral encampment loci and Zenodo Early China and Steppe radiocarbon records [@EarlyChinaC14_2025].

## Non-Stationary Matérn Kriging Calibration

Continuous intra-regional surface allocation across the 26.461 cells employs Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Gaussian random field kriging with Matérn covariance ($\nu = 3/2$) [@paciorek2006spatial]. The spatial correlation function between two locations $s_i$ and $s_j$ incorporates spatially varying local covariance matrices $\Sigma(s)$:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma^2 |\Sigma(s_i)|^{1/4} |\Sigma(s_j)|^{1/4} \left| \frac{\Sigma(s_i) + \Sigma(s_j)}{2} \right|^{-1/2} \frac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)} (2 \sqrt{\nu} Q_{ij})^\nu K_\nu(2 \sqrt{\nu} Q_{ij})$$

where Mahalanobis distance $Q_{ij} = \sqrt{(s_i - s_j)^T \left( \frac{\Sigma(s_i) + \Sigma(s_j)}{2} \right)^{-1} (s_i - s_j)}$. Calibration relies on 87.810 East Asian domestic site records across 1.074 catchments, regularised with spatial bandwidth $\tau_1 = 1,50$ and $\tau_2 = 2,775$ [@paciorek2006spatial]. Table \ref{tab:kriging-steppe} summarises variogram model diagnostics across ten archaeological calibration horizons.

```{r tab-kriging, results='asis'}
ea_labels <- c(
  palaeolithic_early_neolithic = "1. Palaeolithic and Early Neolithic (pre-5000BC)",
  middle_neolithic_yangshao = "2. Middle Neolithic Yangshao (5000 to 3000BC)",
  late_neolithic_longshan = "3. Late Neolithic Longshan (3000 to 2000BC)",
  bronze_age_shang_zhou = "4. Bronze Age Shang and Western Zhou (2000 to 771BC)",
  spring_autumn_warring_states = "5. Spring and Autumn and Warring States (770 to 221BC)",
  qin_han_xiongnu = "6. Qin, Han and Xiongnu Horizon (221BC to 220AD)",
  wei_jin_northern_southern = "7. Wei-Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties (220 to 589AD)",
  sui_tang_five_dynasties = "8. Sui, Tang and Turkic-Uyghur Horizon (581 to 960AD)",
  liao_song_jin_yuan = "9. Liao, Song, Jin and Mongol Horizon (907 to 1368AD)",
  ming_qing_imperial = "10. Ming and Qing Imperial Horizon (1368 to 1912AD)"
)
ea_horizons <- names(diag_data$variogram_models)
krig_df <- data.frame(
  Horizon = unname(ea_labels[ea_horizons]),
  Tau1 = vapply(ea_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$tau1_dimensionless, 2L), character(1)),
  Nugget = vapply(ea_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$c0_nugget, 5L), character(1)),
  Nugget_Sill = vapply(ea_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$nugget_to_sill_ratio, 2L), character(1)),
  Pseudo_R2 = vapply(ea_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$residual_r2, 4L), character(1)),
  Mean_Cell = vapply(ea_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$mean_value, 4L), character(1)),
  P99_Cell = vapply(ea_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$p99_value, 4L), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(krig_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  krig_df,
  "East Asian kriging variogram diagnostics across ten archaeological horizons (163.892 valid land cells, regularised tau1 = 1,50, tau2 = 2,775).",
  c("Kriging Horizon", "Tau1", "Nugget c0", "Nugget-to-Sill", "Residual R²", "Mean Cell", "P99 Cell"),
  list(label = "tab:kriging-steppe", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Regional trend surfaces incorporate environmental and physiographic covariates via weighted least-squares (WLS) regression. Covariate slopes include natural habitat suitability ($\beta_1$), ecozone biomass potential ($\beta_2$), fluvial proximity ($\beta_3$) and coastal-maritime distance ($\beta_4$). Table \ref{tab:kriging-betas-steppe} reports these estimated parameters across all calibration epochs.

```{r tab-kriging-betas, results='asis'}
beta_rows <- lapply(ea_horizons, function(hk) {
  betas <- diag_data$residual_kriging_wls_betas[[hk]]
  data.frame(
    Horizon = unname(ea_labels[[hk]]),
    NatBeta = viscount_fmt_number(betas$beta_1_nat, 4L),
    EcoBeta = viscount_fmt_number(betas$beta_2_eco, 4L),
    FluvBeta = viscount_fmt_number(betas$beta_3_fluvial, 4L),
    CoastBeta = viscount_fmt_number(betas$beta_4_coastal, 4L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
beta_df <- do.call(rbind, beta_rows)
rownames(beta_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  beta_df,
  "Weighted least-squares environmental covariate slopes across ten East Asian kriging calibration horizons.",
  c("Horizon", "Natural Beta", "Ecozone Beta", "Fluvial Beta", "Coastal Beta"),
  list(label = "tab:kriging-betas-steppe", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Trajectory and Share Dynamics

Figure \ref{fig:traj-steppe} depicts the aggregate population curve for Mongolia from 10000BC to 1206AD alongside regional trajectories and a conservative $\pm 8\%$ uncertainty envelope. Growth proceeded in distinct pulses: modest hunter-gatherer expansion prior to 3000BC, a quadrupling across the Bronze Age pastoral transition (3000BC to 500BC), an imperial surge under the Xiongnu peaking around 0AD, stagnation and volatility during post-Xiongnu political fragmentation, and sustained mediaeval expansion under the Uyghur Khaganate and Khitan Liao administration leading into the 1206AD Mongol unification.

```{r fig-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_steppe_prehistory_and_nomadic_empires_trajectory.png",
  "Population trajectory of Mongolia from 10000BC to 1206AD with sub-regional hydro-basin curves and uncertainty band.",
  "fig:traj-steppe"
)
```

Regional share distributions illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:shares-steppe} confirm the shifting balance of demographic weight across ecological zones. Throughout prehistory, the Orkhon-Selenge forest-steppe and the Khangai highlands maintained commanding shares, together accounting for 48% to 54% of all inhabitants. In contrast, the Southern Gobi desert-steppe declined steadily in relative weight from 10% in 10000BC to 11% in 1206AD despite modest absolute growth, reflecting severe hydrological constraints on pastoral herd expansion.

```{r fig-shares, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_steppe_prehistory_and_nomadic_empires_shares.png",
  "Changing demographic shares across the six Mongolian hydro-basins between 10000BC and 1206AD.",
  "fig:shares-steppe"
)
```

# Regional Demographic Trajectories

## Orkhon-Selenge Forest-Steppe Basin

Covering 168.883 km² across north-central Mongolia, the Orkhon-Selenge basin forms the primary agricultural and pastoral artery of the steppe. The confluence of the Selenge, Orkhon and Tuul rivers creates extensive alluvial floodplains bordered by productive larch-pine mountain forests [@Lerch2022Holocene]. Population increased from 4.000 in 10000BC to 20.000 in 2000BC, reached 115.000 under the Xiongnu in 0AD, and expanded to 210.000 by 1206AD.

During the Xiongnu period, this basin accommodated agricultural and metallurgical settlements such as Boroo Gol (peaking at 3,5k), Gua Dov (5,0k) and elite burial grounds at Noyon Uul (3,2k) [@honeychurch2014inner; @brosseder2011xiongnu]. Investigations at Boroo Gol demonstrate extensive grain storage pits containing carbonized broomcorn millet (*Panicum miliaceum*), iron ploughshares and cast-iron pot fragments, revealing that agricultural production was systematically integrated into the nomadic political economy [@Zhang2021Pastoralism]. In mediaeval times, the Khitan Liao transformed the lower Orkhon and Tuul valleys into a garrison zone, erecting massive rammed-earth fortresses including Khar Bukh Balgas (7,5k) and Khermen Denzh (5,5k) [@bemmann2011complex]. By 1206AD, density reached 1,24 persons per km², the highest on the plateau.

## Khangai Central Highlands and Tamir-Khanuy

The Khangai highlands (210.992 km²) encompass the sacred heartland of nomadic statecraft (*Ötüken*), encompassing the upper Orkhon, Tamir, Khanuy and Chuluut river systems [@golden1992introduction]. Sheltered intermontane valleys provided premium winter pastures, supporting demographic growth from 3.500 in 10000BC to 20.000 in 2000BC, 42.000 in 1000BC and 100.000 in 0AD.

This region contains the highest density of monumental Bronze Age mortuary architecture, including the Urt Bulagyn and Khanuy Valley khirigsuurs [@Taylor2019Radiocarbon; @houle2010emergent]. At Urt Bulagyn, excavations revealed over 1.700 peripheral horse burial mounds surrounding a single colossal central mound, documenting the mass sacrifice of prime riding stallions during funeral feasts [@Taylor2019Radiocarbon]. The region also features Xiongnu elite complexes at Gol Mod 1 and Gol Mod 2 [@brosseder2011xiongnu], and the Turkic royal monuments of Bilge Khagan and Kül Tegin at Khoshoo Tsaidam (peaking at 6,0k) [@golden1992introduction].

Under the Uyghur Khaganate, the grand capital of Khar Balgas (Ordu-Baliq) expanded to 48k residents, serving as the largest urban centre on the eastern steppe prior to Karakorum [@bemmann2011complex]. Khitan Liao garrisons at Chin Tolgoi (14k peak) maintained intensive administrative control, elevating basin population to 147.000 by 1206AD (density 0,70 persons per km²).

## Kherlen-Onon Eastern Steppe Basin

Spanning 299.514 km² eastward to the Khingan foothills, the Kherlen-Onon basin consists of rolling feather-grass steppe well suited to large-scale horse and cattle pastoralism [@A2025Patterns; @J2025Slab]. Human numbers grew from 2.500 in 10000BC to 18.000 in 2000BC, 35.000 in 1000BC and 60.000 in 0AD, rising to 126.000 by 1206AD.

In the Bronze Age, this basin served as the core of the Slab Grave culture, whose stone box burials spread westward into central Mongolia [@J2025Slab]. Important mortuary series at Ulaanzuukh (2,2k peak) and Tavan Tolgoi demonstrate continuous pastoral occupation [@J2025Slab; @Jeong2020Dynamic]. Under the Xiongnu, fortified outposts like Tereljiin Dorvoljin (6,5k peak) guarded eastern trade routes [@honeychurch2014inner].

The Khitan Liao established their northern administrative citadel at Kherlen Bars (11k peak), featuring monumental earthen ramparts and an octagonal brick stupa [@bemmann2011complex]. Excavations at Kherlen Bars have recovered architectural roof tiles, cast-bronze seals and agricultural sickle blades confirming permanent garrison life [@bemmann2011complex]. In the twelfth century, the upper Kherlen and Onon rivers nurtured the Khamag Mongol confederation, providing the demographic base for Temüjin's political unification.

## Altai Mountains and Great Lakes Depression

Occupying 297.051 km² in western Mongolia, this region combines glaciated Altai alpine pastures with endorheic lake depressions (Uvs Nuur, Khyargas Nuur, Khar-Us Nuur) [@AR2022Spread]. Pastoralism took root early through Afanasievo and Chemurchek migrations from southern Siberia and Xinjiang [@Jeong2018Bronze; @AR2022Spread]. Population increased from 2.500 in 10000BC to 15.000 in 2000BC, 35.000 in 1000BC and 70.000 in 0AD, expanding to 105.000 by 1206AD.

Key sites include the Chandman culture cemetery at Ulaangom (2,2k peak), Altai deer stone complexes, and stratified petroglyphs recording transhumant horse herding [@Ganbaatar2023Issue; @AR2022Spread]. Radiocarbon determinations from Ulaangom establish an Iron Age transition characterized by bronze weaponry, equestrian harness gear and cranial trepanation [@AR2022Spread]. The region maintained strong cultural connections with the Pazyryk culture of the Gorny Altai and later served as the territory of the Naiman confederation prior to 1206AD.

## Southern Gobi Desert-Steppe and Oases

Covering 496.815 km² along the southern border of Mongolia, the Gobi basin consists of semi-desert scrub, gravel plains (*gobi*) and localized artesian springs [@Lerch2022Holocene]. Severe aridity limited prehistoric hunter-gatherers and pastoralists alike. Aggregate numbers rose from 1.500 in 10000BC to 8.000 in 2000BC, 20.000 in 1000BC and 50.000 in 0AD, reaching 77.000 by 1206AD.

Human settlement clustered around oases, camel caravan routes, and copper extraction nodes like Oyuun Tolgoi [@Almathen2016Ancient; @Bennett2017Taming]. At Bayanzag (Flaming Cliffs), Epipalaeolithic core and blade caches document early desert hunter-gatherer presence. In historical times, southern Gobi encampments facilitated vital communication links between the steppe khaganates and the Hexi corridor, providing dromedary transport for long-distance luxury trade [@Almathen2016Ancient]. Despite comprising nearly a third of Mongolia's total land area, extreme ecological limits held terminal density to 0,15 persons per km².

## Lake Khövsgöl and Darkhad Boreal Taiga

Covering 89.221 km² in northernmost Mongolia, this mountainous sub-arctic region encompasses the tectonic rift basin of Lake Khövsgöl and the Darkhad lacustrine depression [@Taylor2019Investigating]. Subsistence relied on sub-taiga horse and cattle herding, forest hunting, lake fishing and high-altitude cervid exploitation [@Taylor2019Investigating]. Population expanded from 1.000 in 10000BC to 4.000 in 2000BC, 8.000 in 1000BC and 25.000 in 0AD, reaching 35.000 by 1206AD (density 0,39 persons per km²).

Ice-patch archaeology in the Darkhad depression has recovered organic cultural material including birchbark arrows, wooden composite bows and carved bone points dating from 1500BC onward [@Taylor2019Investigating]. These finds demonstrate that northern populations retained specialized boreal foraging and reindeer herding strategies while interacting continuously with southern steppe pastoralists [@Taylor2019Investigating]. Key mortuary and residential sites at Salkhityn-Am (2,2k peak), Arbulag and Ulaan-Uul confirm persistent mountain-valley occupation throughout the late Holocene.

```{r tab-regions, results='asis'}
yr_cols <- c("-10000", "-3000", "-1000", "-200", "0", "750", "1206")
col_labels <- c("10000BC", "3000BC", "1000BC", "200BC", "0AD", "750AD", "1206AD")
reg_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[[y]]), character(1))
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  df_r <- data.frame(
    Region = nm,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(rv$area_km2, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
    df_r[[col_labels[idx]]] <- vals[idx]
  }
  df_r
})
reg_df <- do.call(rbind, reg_rows)

tot_vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) {
  sum_y <- sum(vapply(mod_data$regions, function(r) as.numeric(r$population[[y]]), numeric(1)))
  viscount_fmt_pop(sum_y)
}, character(1))

tot_row <- data.frame(
  Region = "Module Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$total_area_km2, 0L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
  tot_row[[col_labels[idx]]] <- tot_vals[idx]
}
reg_df <- rbind(reg_df, tot_row)
rownames(reg_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  reg_df,
  "Sub-regional population benchmarks across the six Mongolian macro-basins from 10000BC to 1206AD.",
  c("Hydro-Basin", "Area (km²)", col_labels),
  list(label = "tab:regions-steppe", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Table \ref{tab:density-steppe} summarises the distribution of the 437 catalogued settlements and monument complexes (2.795 settlement-year observations, mean 6,40 per centre) alongside benchmark populations and terminal 1206AD pastoral densities. Site coverage is led by the Khangai Central Highlands (97 sites), Altai Great Lakes Basin (88), Gobi Southern Desert Steppe (82) and Orkhon-Selenge Forest Steppe (78). The Orkhon-Selenge basin supported the highest human density (1,24 persons per km²), followed by the Khangai highlands (0,70) and Kherlen-Onon (0,42).

```{r tab-density, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
dens_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  ar <- as.numeric(rv$area_km2)
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  n_sites <- sum(vapply(sett_data, function(s) identical(s$region_id, rk), logical(1)))
  p_10000bc <- as.numeric(rv$population[["-10000"]])
  p_1206ad <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1206"]])
  data.frame(
    Region = nm,
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
    P10000BC = viscount_fmt_pop(p_10000bc),
    P1206AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1206ad),
    D1206AD = viscount_fmt_number(p_1206ad / ar, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
dens_df <- do.call(rbind, dens_rows)
rownames(dens_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  dens_df,
  "Catalogued settlements (n=437), 10000BC and 1206AD population benchmarks and terminal 1206AD pastoral density (persons per km²).",
  c("Hydro-Basin", "Sites", "10000BC", "1206AD", "1206AD (km²)"),
  list(label = "tab:density-steppe", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Discussion

## The Dairy Revolution and Demographic Expansion

Demographic expansion across prehistoric Mongolia demonstrates the primary role of subsistence technology in overcoming ecological bottlenecks [@Taylor2020Early; @Jeong2018Bronze]. Without domesticated livestock, terminal Pleistocene foragers were constrained by primary plant productivity and wild herd reproductive cycles, holding aggregate numbers below 30k for over four millennia. The introduction of ruminant dairy pastoralism between 3000BC and 2000BC enabled human groups to convert cellulosic steppe grasses into easily digestible proteins, fats and milk sugars [@Wilkin2020Dairy; @S2024Cauldrons].

Ancient DNA analyses reveal that this early pastoral transition occurred through localized cultural transmission alongside genetic admixture [@Jeong2018Bronze; @J2025Slab]. Indigenous north-east Asian foragers incorporated Afanasievo herding practices while preserving distinct genetic lineages until the Middle to Late Bronze Age, when Slab Grave populations expanded westward from the eastern steppe [@J2025Slab]. Dairying provided a renewable, non-lethal food source that insulated human populations against seasonal starvation, enabling population to double every eight to ten centuries between 3000BC and 500BC.

Proteomic analyses of dental calculus demonstrate the sequential adoption of diverse animal milks [@Wilkin2020Dairy; @S2024Cauldrons]. Initial Bronze Age dairying focused on sheep, goats and cattle, but by 1200BC horse milk peptides (*Equus caballus*) appear regularly, indicating the milking of mares [@Wilkin2020Dairy]. Fermented mare's milk (*airag* / *koumiss*) furnished essential vitamin C and calories during summer pasturing without requiring grain consumption [@S2024Cauldrons]. Furthermore, bronze cauldrons from Khangai ritual sites have yielded yak milk proteins (*Bos grunniens*), confirming high-altitude livestock diversification across northern mountain pastures [@S2024Cauldrons].

## Urban Enclaves Within Mobile Pastoral Regimes

A persistent debate in steppe historiography concerns the nature and sustainability of urbanism in nomadic empires [@rogers2012inner; @sneath2007headless]. Sedentary urban settlements on the steppe were not organic market towns generated by agricultural surplus; rather, they functioned as specialized imperial instruments constructed by royal decree to facilitate political administration, taxation, foreign diplomacy and elite consumption [@barfield1989perilous; @bemmann2011complex].

The spatial catalogue of 437 settlements illustrates this institutional pattern. In the Xiongnu period, fortified sites like Gua Dov and Boroo Gol served as agricultural depots and metallurgical workshops operated by Han defectors and captives [@honeychurch2014inner; @Zhang2021Pastoralism]. Under the Uyghurs, Khar Balgas emerged as a monumental political metropolis, housing 48k inhabitants supported by grain imported from surrounding irrigated fields and southern Chinese tributaries [@bemmann2011complex]. Archaeological surveys at Khar Balgas reveal rammed-earth ramparts rising over 10 metres, a square citadel with internal palace courtyards, brick-paved ceremonial roads and specialized craft production quarters for iron, bronze and ceramics [@bemmann2011complex].

Even within these massive earthen enclosures, royal and aristocratic quarters retained traditional tent platforms (*ger*), demonstrating that mobile ideological traditions coexisted with sedentary architectural forms [@bemmann2011complex; @sneath2007headless]. When imperial authority collapsed, as occurred following the Kyrgyz sack of Khar Balgas in 840AD, these urban populations vanished rapidly, reverting to mobile pastoral life. The Khitan Liao revived this strategy by creating garrison forts at Chin Tolgoi and Kherlen Bars, introducing Bohai and Chinese agricultural colonists who were evacuated or assimilated once Liao control dissolved [@bemmann2011complex]. At Chin Tolgoi, double rectangular earthen defensive perimeters enclosing 140 hectares sheltered an estimated garrison and civilian contingent of 14k persons, complete with ceramic kilns and storage granaries [@bemmann2011complex].

## Paleoclimatic Oscillations and Dzud Frequency

Pastoral population trajectories in Mongolia were intimately coupled with multi-decadal climatic anomalies recorded in high-resolution tree-ring and speleothem archives across northern Eurasia [@Schulte2022Larix; @Lerch2022Holocene]. Episodes of prolonged spring drought followed by severe winter icing (*dzud*) decimated horse and sheep herds, reducing regional carrying capacity by 30% to 50% within single seasons [@M2025Bioavailable; @houle2010emergent].

Such ecological shocks frequently coincided with major sociopolitical transformations [@barfield1989perilous]. The mid-sixth-century climatic cooling associated with the Late Antique Little Ice Age (536-660AD) corresponds to the collapse of the Rouran Khaganate and the rapid consolidation of the First Turkic Khaganate, whose cavalry forces expanded southward to secure Chinese agrarian tribute [@golden1992introduction]. Conversely, the ninth-century megadrought documented across Inner Asia undermined Uyghur irrigated agriculture at Khar Balgas, predisposing the urban citadel to catastrophic defeat by the Yenisei Kyrgyz in 840AD [@bemmann2011complex; @Lerch2022Holocene].

## Environmental Thresholds and the 1206AD Unification

The expansion of Mongolian population to 700k by 1206AD approached the upper carrying capacity of traditional pasture management under non-industrial conditions [@barfield1989perilous; @honeychurch2014inner]. With an average livestock ratio of four to six sheep-equivalent units per person, a human population of 700k required supporting herds of 3,5M to 4,2M head of livestock. In years of severe winter ice crusts (*dzud*) or protracted summer droughts, forage shortfalls provoked acute inter-tribal competition over river valleys and winter campsites [@Lerch2022Holocene; @M2025Bioavailable].

This ecological tension intensified twelfth-century warfare among the Khamag Mongol, Kereit, Naiman and Tatar confederations [@sneath2007headless]. The unification achieved by Temüjin at the 1206AD Kurultai overcame these localized carrying capacity constraints through institutional reorganisation: breaking hereditary tribal aristocracies, instituting a decimal military hierarchy, and channelling internal raiding outward into continental conquest across Eurasia [@barfield1989perilous; @sneath2007headless]. By creating the *Keshik* imperial bodyguard and establishing the Great Yassa legal framework, Genghis Khan replaced segmentary tribal competition with an imperial administrative structure capable of governing continental populations [@barfield1989perilous; @sneath2007headless].

The decimal recruitment system organised pastoral society into units of tens, hundreds, thousands and ten thousands (*tümen*), shattering ancestral clan boundaries and redistributing mobile families across designated pasture territories [@barfield1989perilous; @sneath2007headless]. This administrative rationalisation eliminated localized pasture disputes by enforcing state-level seasonal migration schedules and reserving upland hayfields for imperial horse post stations (*örtöö*). The unified state transformed Mongolia's demographic potential from localized pasture competition into a continental imperial expansion. Table \ref{tab:source-corpora-steppe} details the primary archaeological and historical corpora underlying the broader East Asian spatial kriging domain. For Mongolia specifically, the settlement ledger evaluated 645 candidate localities—integrating archaeological registers with OSM/Wikidata Mongolian archaeological sites, river-valley pastoral encampment loci and Zenodo Early China and Steppe radiocarbon records [@EarlyChinaC14_2025]—retaining 437 validated centres (2.795 settlement-year observations, mean 6,40 per centre) and excluding 208 duplicates or unconfirmed surface scatters (0 unaccounted). Ephemeral mobile pastoral camps remain archaeologically under-represented relative to walled enclosures and stone monuments, motivating reliance on multi-proxy regional carrying-capacity baselines alongside point records.

```{r tab-source-corpora, results='asis'}
src_labels <- c(
  hosner_2016_pangaea = "Hosner et al. East Asian Archaeological Radiocarbon Corpus (PANGAEA)",
  cn_national_key_relics = "National Cultural Heritage Administration Key Protected Sites Registry",
  chgis_v6_time_series = "China Historical GIS (CHGIS v6) Imperial Administrative Settlements",
  chgis_v6_1820_towns = "CHGIS v6 Historical Market Towns and Frontier Outposts (1820AD)",
  aadr_v66 = "Allen Ancient DNA Resource (AADR v66) Eastern Steppe Skeletal Series",
  xronos_c14 = "XRONOS Global Archaeological Radiocarbon Database (East Asian Sector)",
  p3k14c_2025 = "PEOPLE 3000 Radiocarbon Synthesis (Eastern Eurasia Sector)",
  c14bazAAR_dedup = "Deduplicated Global Radiocarbon Synthesis (c14bazAAR)",
  arch_atlas_excavations = "Archaeological Atlas of Inner Asia Excavated Complexes",
  taiwan_boch_heritage = "Taiwan Bureau of Cultural Heritage Heritage Register",
  kham_tibet_monasteries = "Kham and Tibetan Plateau Monastic Settlement Gazetteer",
  polaris_ia_ras_frontier = "Institute of Archaeology RAS Siberian and Altai Frontier Registry",
  mongolia_steppe_archaeology = "Mongolian National Archaeological Registry of Walled Enclosures"
)
sc_keys <- names(meta_data$source_record_counts)
sc_rows <- lapply(sc_keys, function(sk) {
  lbl <- if (sk %in% names(src_labels)) unname(src_labels[[sk]]) else sk
  cnt <- as.numeric(meta_data$source_record_counts[[sk]])
  data.frame(
    Corpus = lbl,
    Records = viscount_fmt_number(cnt, 0L),
    Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * cnt / sum(as.numeric(unlist(meta_data$source_record_counts))), 2L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sc_df <- do.call(rbind, sc_rows)
rownames(sc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sc_df,
  "Component archaeological, radiocarbon and historical registries aggregated into the East Asian kriging domain (87.810 unique domestic records).",
  c("Source Registry", "Raw Records", "Share"),
  list(label = "tab:source-corpora-steppe", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```
